SDE.name: Event Exchange Framework
SDE.description: A platform for moving live data between systems that were never built to talk — 10 interchangeable worker types, shipped in two languages, on clustered Kafka and Redis, and proven with a purpose-built 15-run benchmark.
highlights: Built an event-streaming platform that integrates systems with no shared interface, delivering 10 interchangeable worker types across ingestion, transformation and delivery.
Shipped and maintained parity implementations in Python and TypeScript so teams could choose a runtime without changing the operational model, config format or extension contract.
Designed a declarative worker model where one container image serves any role from config alone, with configuration held in Redis so running instances are repointed without a rebuild.
Built a benchmarking stack with JMeter, Logstash, Elasticsearch and Kibana measuring throughput, end-to-end latency and per-worker load across 15 runs, three cluster shapes and a 5× dataset range.
Established that doubling the processing tier changed throughput under 1% while cutting latency ~2.4×, redirecting optimisation effort away from the tier the team assumed was the bottleneck.
SDE.overview:
Event Exchange moves live data between systems that were never designed to talk to each other. A team connects a source, describes how the data should be reshaped, points it at a destination — and the platform handles buffering, retries, failures and scale underneath.

It ships as a kit rather than a single pipeline: ten interchangeable worker types across three stages, assembled into whatever route a use case needs. I built it end to end, shipped it in two languages, then built a second system whose only job was to find out whether it actually held up under load.

  • 10 worker types — HTTP endpoints, scheduled pollers, live video stream capture, routing, transformation, and delivery to APIs, search indexes and streaming playlists
  • 2 full implementations — Python and TypeScript with matching contracts, so a team picks the runtime that fits without relearning the platform
  • Clustered infrastructure — multi-node Kafka and Redis, containerised, deployed across multiple hosts
  • 15-run benchmark — a purpose-built measurement stack answering whether the design scaled, and where it stopped
SDE.hld:
The shape is deliberately boring in the middle: every stage is separated from the next by a queue. Receivers never call processors, processors never call senders. Nothing in the pipeline knows what comes after it.

That buys the properties that matter operationally. A slow or failing destination applies no backpressure to ingestion — events accumulate in a topic instead of being dropped or timing out at the edge. Any stage can be restarted, scaled or redeployed without coordinating with its neighbours. And because Kafka retains rather than consumes, a stage that was down comes back and works through the backlog.

Message identity and ordering

Every event carries a ULID as its message key, in a header that travels with it the whole way. ULIDs are lexicographically sortable by creation time, which makes a trace of one event's journey readable without joining on timestamps — that turned out to matter more than I expected once benchmarking started.

Partitioning is caller-controlled. Producers may supply a partition key at the ingest endpoint; when they do, every downstream stage propagates that same key when it republishes. The consequence is the useful part: events sharing a key keep their relative order across the entire pipeline, not just within one hop. When no key is supplied, events distribute across partitions and ordering is not promised — which is the right default for independent events, and the wrong one for a per-entity update stream. Choosing that is left to the caller because only the caller knows which they have.

Failure behaviour

A worker that throws while handling an event republishes the original payload — headers and partition key intact — to a dedicated retry topic, then continues consuming. Two things follow from that choice.

The failure is preserved rather than discarded, and it is preserved with enough context to replay it: same key, same headers, same body. And one bad event cannot wedge the pipeline, because the consumer does not block or crash on it.

Replay is deliberately an operator decision — a worker can be pointed at the retry topic to drain it — rather than an automatic loop. Automatic replay without a bound is how a poison message becomes an infinite cycle.

Delivery semantics, and the tradeoff I would revisit

The design targets at-least-once: the retry path means handled failures are kept, and the producer is not configured for idempotence, so a republish can produce a duplicate. Consumers therefore have to tolerate seeing an event twice — that is a real constraint the design pushes onto rule authors, and it should be stated plainly rather than glossed.

Offsets commit on the client's default interval rather than explicitly after a rule completes. That favours throughput and keeps the consume loop simple, at the cost of a narrow window where a hard crash could advance past an event still in flight.

If I were tightening the guarantee, the order would be: commit offsets manually after the rule returns, enable producer idempotence, and give the retry topic an attempt counter with backoff so replay is bounded. Each of those trades some throughput or latency for strictness — which is exactly the conversation worth having with whoever owns the SLA, rather than a decision to make silently in the framework.

Deployment

Kafka runs as a multi-node cluster in KRaft mode, so there is no ZooKeeper ensemble to operate alongside it. Redis runs clustered with replicas, distributing keys across hash slots. Both are containerised, authenticated, and were deployed split across multiple hosts during benchmarking to make sure nothing depended on colocation.
SDE.lld:
A worker is config plus one function

A processor's entire wiring — which queue it reads, which it writes, which consumer group it joins, where failures go — is a short config file:

MINION_NAME:    relay1
CONSUMER_GROUP: PROCESSORS
CONSUME_TOPIC:  DEMO_RECEIVED
PRODUCE_TOPIC:  DEMO_PROCESSED
RETRY_TOPIC:    DEMO_RETRY

Behaviour comes from a separate rules file exposing exactly one hook:

async def execute_rules(json_data, received_topic, e2_util) -> dict:
    ...

That signature is the contract, and the boundary it draws is the whole design. The framework owns transport, retries, logging, configuration and lifecycle. The rules file owns the transformation and nothing else. Returning None drops the event deliberately; raising sends it to the retry topic.

The same container image becomes a different worker from config alone. Because that config lives in Redis rather than baked into the image, a running instance can be repointed without a rebuild or redeploy. Getting that boundary right is what made ten worker types maintainable instead of ten codebases.

Two runtimes held to one contract

The framework exists twice. The Python and TypeScript trees carry the same ten workers and the same four connectors — Kafka, Redis, Elasticsearch, HTTP — down to matching logging configuration. A team picks the runtime that suits the workload without changing the operational model, the config format or the extension contract.

Keeping parity is a real ongoing cost. It is worth it because the alternative — one runtime, and a rewrite whenever a use case does not fit it — is a worse cost paid later.

Building something that could tell the truth

Building the platform was half the work. The other half was building a system that could measure it honestly.

Every worker emits structured logs keyed by test, worker and message identifier. Logstash parses those as they arrive, Elasticsearch indexes them, and Kibana computes four KPIs live: system throughput, end-to-end latency, per-worker processing time, and load distribution across the fleet. JMeter drives stepped load from three concurrent producers.

Because the message key travels end to end, a single event's full path is queryable — which is what makes end-to-end latency a measurement rather than an estimate.

Then fifteen runs: three cluster shapes against five dataset sizes spanning a 5× range, distributed across multiple hosts.

What the numbers said — including the part I did not expect

Doubling the processing and delivery tiers changed throughput by under 1%. The obvious lever did almost nothing. At every dataset size, the baseline and the double-capacity configuration landed within a percent of each other.

What did change was responsiveness: end-to-end latency fell roughly 2.4×. The extra capacity drained queues faster without lifting the ceiling.

Adding deliberately expensive transformation logic cost about 2%, so the work the platform was doing was not the constraint either. And throughput fell by roughly a third as the dataset grew 5×, so the system was not holding a flat rate under sustained load.

The open question

Those results locate a ceiling without explaining it. Two things were held constant across all fifteen runs — the ingest tier and the load generator itself — which makes them the obvious suspects. But that is an inference, not a result, and I will not present it as a finding.

The experiments that would settle it are straightforward: vary partition count independently of consumer count to test whether queue parallelism is the real cap, scale the ingest tier while holding everything downstream fixed, and drive load from hardware that is not itself a plausible bottleneck.

I would rather ship a measured negative result and name the next experiment than a confident story the data does not support.

SDE.name: Video Analytics Project
SDE.description: Site surveillance for a fuel-retail operator: four RTSP cameras sampled to Kafka, face detection running as a stream consumer, and flagged frames pushed to an operator's browser over WebSockets. Built on an earlier version of the Event Exchange Framework, which it extended with a video-capture worker type.
highlights: Built a camera-to-browser violation detection system on the Event Exchange Framework, extending it with a stream-producer worker type that samples RTSP feeds with OpenCV and publishes frames as Kafka events.
Split each camera onto two topics so the live-view lane and the detection lane run as independent consumer groups, keeping the operator live feed at full rate regardless of detection lag.
Ran detection as a single relay consuming all four camera topics and republishing only frames containing a detection, so the storage tier is sized for detections rather than for ingest.

Built the FastAPI + SQLModel + MariaDB backend and React/Redux client: JWT auth, per-camera WebSocket fan-out for live frames, and a violation gallery over disk-stored JPEGs with a bounded retention window.

Deployed seven pipeline containers and a three-tier app stack against a 3-node Kafka (KRaft) and 6-node Redis cluster, with each worker config held in Redis so instances are repointed without a rebuild.
SDE.overview:
A surveillance system for a fuel-retail operator's forecourts. Four fixed cameras across two sites are sampled continuously; each frame travels through a Kafka pipeline to a detector, and anything the detector flags lands in an operator's browser as a timestamped, reviewable still.

It runs on an earlier version of the Event Exchange Framework — my own event-streaming platform — and extending it was part of the work: video needed a worker type the framework did not have, one that opens an RTSP stream and turns it into events. Things the framework grew later — ULID message keys, a dedicated retry topic — are not in the version deployed here, so the failure behaviour described below is the earlier, simpler version of it.

The system runs two lanes side by side, and keeping them separate is the whole design:

  • Live lane — every sampled frame from every camera, pushed straight to whoever is watching. Nothing analyses it; it just has to arrive.
  • Violation lane — the same frames, but through the detector. Only frames with a detection continue, get written to disk and the database, and appear in the violation gallery.

On what the detector actually is: the version in this repo runs dlib's frontal-face detector — a classical HOG + linear-SVM model, not a deep network — configured as a violation type called FACE_DETECTED. The detector is a pluggable stage rather than the point of the system: the pipeline around it treats "what counts as a violation" as configuration, and face detection was the first thing wired through it end to end.
SDE.hld:
The camera never talks to the detector, and the detector never talks to the browser. Every stage is separated from the next by a Kafka topic, which is what makes the two lanes independent instead of merely parallel.

Why each camera publishes twice

Each capture service publishes every sampled frame to two topics: its own per-camera topic, and a shared live topic. That looks redundant until you ask what happens when detection gets slow.

The detector consumes the per-camera topics. The live-view forwarder consumes the shared topic. They are separate consumer groups with separate offsets, so a detector that falls behind — a heavier model, a stalled container, a restart — accumulates lag on its own topics and nothing else. The operator's live view keeps running at full rate, because nothing in its path is waiting on inference. Had both lanes shared one stream, every second of detection latency would have been a second of live-view latency.

Fan-in, not fan-out

One relay service subscribes to all four camera topics at once and merges them into a single stream — the framework's consume-topic setting splits on commas, so this is configuration, not code. Frames carry their own camera and site identity in the payload, so a merged stream loses nothing.

That relay is also the filter. It republishes to the violations topic only when the detector fires. Everything downstream — the writer, the database, the disk — is sized for detections rather than for ingest, which is the difference between storing what matters and storing every frame from every camera forever.

Failure behaviour

Because Kafka retains rather than consumes, a stage that dies comes back and works through its backlog from its committed offset; the frames it missed are still there. Containers are declared restart: always, so recovery is the default state rather than an operator action.

The pipeline is deliberately lossy at the edge and lossless after it. The capture service samples one frame per second and discards the rest of the stream before anything is published — the camera runs at full frame rate, the pipeline does not. That sampling is the real backpressure control: it fixes the ingest rate at the one place where dropping data is cheap and obvious, instead of letting a queue silently decide later.

Configuration lives outside the container

Each service loads its YAML config once at startup and writes it into a Redis cluster, then reads every setting back from Redis at runtime. Two consequences follow. A running instance can be repointed — different topic, different violation type — by changing a key, with no rebuild. And because each service registers itself in a per-type set on startup and removes its own keys on shutdown, Redis doubles as a live inventory of what is actually running, which is otherwise surprisingly hard to answer for a fleet of identical containers.

What the app tier guarantees

The backend holds one WebSocket channel per camera and broadcasts to whoever is attached to it. Live frames are pushed; violations are polled, because a violation is a record with a row and a file behind it, and the client wants the newest N rather than a stream.

Storage is explicitly bounded, not archival: after each write the oldest records past a fixed retention count are deleted, file and row together. This is a monitoring console, not evidence retention — and a bounded store that cannot fill the disk was the right trade for an on-site box.

Access scoping — and what it is not

Each user is bound to a site, and the client fetches only that site's cameras, so an operator at one forecourt does not see another's feeds. This is site-scoped access, not role-based access control — there is no role model in the schema. Calling it RBAC would overstate what is implemented.
SDE.lld:
The event on the wire

Every message in the pipeline is one JSON object describing one frame:

  • frame — the image, JPEG-encoded then base64'd
  • camera_id, camera_model
  • site_id, site_location, site_region
  • violation_type — "NA" until a detector sets it
  • timestamp — capture time

Base64-over-JSON was a deliberate trade, and it is the one I would revisit first. It costs roughly a third more bytes on every message than the raw JPEG would, and image payloads on a broker is not what a broker is for. What it buys is uniformity: every worker in the framework is a plain JSON transform, one deserialiser, one contract, no binary serde and no second storage system to keep in sync with the event stream. At four cameras and one frame per second that trade is comfortable; it is the first thing that stops being comfortable as cameras are added, and the fix — put the bytes in object storage, put a reference on the topic — is well understood.

Capture

OpenCV opens the RTSP URL and reads frames in a loop. A frame is only encoded and published once the configured gap since the last published frame has elapsed (GAP_BETWEEN_FRAMES: 1 second in this deployment); everything in between is read and dropped. Site and camera identity are attached at publish time from config, so adding a camera is a new config file and a compose entry, not new code — the four capture services are the same program with different configuration.

Detection

The relay decodes base64 → JPEG bytes → OpenCV matrix, scales the longest edge to 640px, converts to greyscale and runs dlib.get_frontal_face_detector() at one upsample pass. Each hit is drawn as a labelled rectangle onto the frame, and the annotated frame is re-encoded and swapped back into the same JSON object — so what an operator reviews is the frame with the detection marked on it, not a raw still plus coordinates. Consumption is handed to a four-thread pool so decode-detect-encode on one frame does not block reading the next.

Two implementation warts I would fix before this scaled:

  • The republish loop emits one message per detected face, so a frame with three faces produces three identical events and three stored images. The detection count should be a field, not a repeat count.
  • The capture service registers itself under the framework's pull service type although a stream type exists in the enum — harmless at runtime, but it makes the Redis service inventory lie about what is running, which is exactly the thing that inventory is for.

The app tier

FastAPI with SQLModel over MariaDB. Three tables — violation, camera, site — plus users. The write path decodes the frame to a JPEG file on disk and stores the path in the row rather than the image, then upserts the camera and site records so the topology registers itself from the traffic; the read path re-encodes files to base64 for the client. The cleanup pass runs on every write and trims to the newest 50 violations, deleting file and row together.

POST /emit/live/{camera_id}broadcast a frame to that camera's WebSocket subscribers
POST /emit/{camera_id}persist a violation, upsert camera + site, trim old records
GET /frames/{camera_id}?limit=Nnewest N violations, images inlined as base64
GET /cameras/site/{site_id}cameras and site detail for a user's site
WS /ws/live/{camera_id}live frame channel, one per camera

Auth is bcrypt password hashing and an HS256 JWT with a 20-minute expiry; the client re-validates its token on an interval and drops to the login screen the moment the server rejects it, so an expired session cannot sit on screen showing stale frames.

Client

React with Redux Toolkit. On mount it opens one WebSocket per camera and writes incoming frames into a per-camera slice of the store, so switching cameras is a store read rather than a reconnect and the view is populated instantly. The violations tab polls the frames endpoint on an interval and renders a thumbnail strip against a detail pane showing violation type, timestamp and source camera.

Deployment

Two compose stacks against shared middleware. The pipeline stack runs seven containers — four capture services, one detection relay, two forwarders — each bind-mounting the single framework utility file so every worker runs the same copy. The app stack runs the client, the API and MariaDB. Underneath sit a three-node Kafka cluster in KRaft mode (no ZooKeeper) and a six-node Redis cluster, three masters and three replicas, with HAProxy fronting both for access from outside the Docker network.

Startup ordering is handled by staggered sleeps in the container commands — producers first, relay after, forwarders last. It works, and it is the wrong mechanism: these should be health checks and retry-on-connect, so that a slow broker delays startup rather than failing it.

What I would change

  • Frame bytes to object storage, references on the topic.
  • Detection count as a field rather than duplicate messages.
  • Timestamps as UTC ISO-8601 end to end — the current path formats a local-offset string at capture, parses it back at write, and re-localises it, which is three chances to be wrong for no benefit.
  • Bounded work queues in the forwarders; they currently spawn a thread per message, which is fine at this rate and unbounded at any other.
  • Broker and camera credentials out of the config files and into injected secrets.
  • Health checks instead of startup sleeps.

SDE.name: Code Search Engine
SDE.description: Keyword search over 12,297 competitive-programming problems crawled from three sites and ranked by a TF-IDF index built from scratch in Python — searchable by what a problem says, not what it is called.
highlights: Built the retrieval stack from scratch rather than reaching for a search library: a Selenium crawler over three problem sets, a text-normalisation pass, and an inverted index of 36,957 terms and 1,053,417 postings computed in plain Python over 12,297 problems.

Kept links and titles index-aligned with the scored documents so a hit resolves to a clickable problem rather than a document id — and found, on re-reading, that the alignment holds only because the crawler happens to number files contiguously.

Measured the deployed service instead of trusting the code, and found the ranking is discarded in transit: the query script sorts by score and then calls list(set(results)), so the exact match for "longest palindromic substring" ranks 1st locally with that line removed and 248th of 704 live.

Traced the ~6 s query latency to the plumbing rather than the search — a Python process is spawned per request and re-reads a 31.8 MB index, plus a 15 MB corpus file it never uses, taking ~1.1 s to do ~7 ms of scoring.

Found a second user-visible defect in the same pass: digit-stripping meant for the index body was also applied to display titles, damaging 6,328 of 12,297 of them — "Number of 1 Bits" renders as "Number of   Bits".
SDE.overview:
You remember the problem but not its name. Something about a sliding window over a string, on one of three sites, two years ago. Each site's own search wants the title you don't have. This searches the text of the problem instead — type what you remember, get the link.

Underneath it is a retrieval stack written from scratch rather than assembled from a search library, which is the reason it was worth building: a crawler that walks three problem sets, a normalisation pass over the text, and a TF-IDF index computed in plain Python. None of the ranking is delegated to anything.

  • 12,297 problems indexed — 1,999 LeetCode, 6,299 Codeforces, 3,999 CodeChef
  • 36,957 terms and 1,053,417 postings in the inverted index
  • Selenium and BeautifulSoup to crawl, Python to index, Express to serve, React to search from
  • Still deployed — front end on Netlify, API on a free-tier instance, and it still answers

It is also the project I learned the most from by re-reading it. Writing this up meant measuring the live service rather than trusting the code, and the measurements found two defects that make the system look much worse from the outside than it is inside: one line discards the ranking the whole index exists to produce, and another mangles half the titles it displays. Both are documented in full below instead of being quietly fixed and left out. The interesting finding isn't that a hand-written index works — it's that a working index can be completely invisible from the outside.

Live site · Source
SDE.hld:
The system has two halves that never run at the same time, and almost everything worth saying about it follows from where the boundary sits. The left half runs once, offline, and takes hours. The right half runs on every search and should take milliseconds. It doesn't, and the reason is structural rather than algorithmic.

The offline half: crawl, normalise, invert

Two passes per site. The first walks the paginated problem set collecting URLs; the second visits each URL and writes three files — the problem text, its link, and its title — numbered by a counter that only advances on success, so the three directories stay index-aligned even when a page fails.

The cost of that second pass is the thing I would change first. The browser is opened inside the per-page function, so a full headless Chrome is launched and torn down for each of 12,297 problems, with fixed sleeps around the waits on top. One reusable driver would have cut the crawl by most of its runtime for a few lines of restructuring. I have no figure for how long it actually took, because nothing timed it — which is its own finding.

The indexer then does one linear pass to build the postings and document frequencies, and a second to turn them into weights. It is the honest textbook construction, and at this corpus size that is the right call: the whole index builds in one pass over 12,297 short documents and lands as 31.8 MB on disk.

What crosses the gate

Exactly one artefact matters at query time: a JSON object mapping each term to a map of document index to weight. It is a genuine inverted index — a query touches only the postings of the words in it, not the corpus — and that is why scoring is fast. Alongside it sit parallel arrays of links and titles, so a document index resolves to a clickable result rather than a number.

Storing it as one JSON blob is fine for a corpus this size and stops being fine immediately after. There is no way to read part of it.

The per-request half: where the six seconds go

A search posts to an Express endpoint, which spawns a fresh Python process per request. That process loads all four JSON files, scores the query, prints JSON to stdout, and dies. Nothing is cached, nothing is warm, and nothing is shared between two searches a second apart.

Measured on this index:

  • ~1.1 s to load the index from disk
  • ~7 ms to score a query against it
  • ~6 s end-to-end through the deployed API

So the search is roughly a thousandth of the wait. The rest is process startup, re-reading 31.8 MB, and — this one is pure waste — re-reading a further 15 MB cleaned copy of the corpus that the query script binds to a variable and never touches again. The front end apologises to the user with "the dataset is very big so it may take some time"; the dataset is not what they are waiting for. A single long-lived process holding the index in memory turns a six-second search into a fast one without changing one line of the ranking.

Filtering in the wrong place

The API returns the entire ranked list and the React client filters it by looking for the site's name in each URL. A broad query therefore ships around 12,000 rows to the browser so it can show a handful — measured: 9,008 results for two sum, 11,970 for output.

Both fixes are cheap and neither was done: take the top k before returning, and pass the platform selection to the server so it filters before serialising rather than after.

Failure behaviour

This is the weakest part of the design, and worth being precise about because the failure mode is silent rather than loud.

The query script wraps its work in a bare except that calls exit(). So any error exits with status 0 and an empty stdout — a success, as far as the caller can tell. The server checks the exit code, sees zero, tries to parse nothing as JSON, and returns a 500 whose message is a JSON parse error. The real cause never reaches a log at either end.

Two smaller ones in the same area: the server spawns the Python script by a path relative to the current working directory, so where it was started from is part of the contract; and its listen call reads 5000 || process.env.PORT, which can only ever evaluate to 5000 — the environment variable a hosting platform sets is unreachable, and the operands are the wrong way round.

What the shape gets right

Setting the defects aside, two structural decisions hold up. Separating the index build from the query path is correct and is why a query can be fast at all — nothing is computed per request that could have been computed once. And keeping the retrieval in one small Python module behind an HTTP boundary means the ranking can be replaced — BM25, stemming, a real index format — without the front end noticing. The seams are in the right places. What runs through them needs work.
SDE.lld:
The scoring, term by term

Term frequency is a word's count in a document divided by that document's length in words after cleaning. Inverse document frequency is 1 + ln(N / df) over N = 12,297. A query is lowercased, split on whitespace, and each term's postings are summed into a per-document score.

The 1 + is worth pausing on: it guarantees no term is ever worth zero. A word appearing in 12,268 of 12,297 documents still carries a weight of about 1.002 and still drags its entire posting list into the candidate set. That is why searching for output matches 12,268 documents — it is not a bug, but it is the reason a stop-word list is doing load-bearing work that IDF was supposed to do, and the list is hand-written and short.

There is also no normalisation of the accumulated score by query length or document vector magnitude — this is a sum of weights, not a cosine. For same-length queries the ranking is unaffected; it means scores aren't comparable across queries, which matters the moment anyone wants a relevance threshold.

The one line that discards the ranking

This is the finding. The query script sorts candidates by descending score, walks that order building link + "*" + title strings — and then does:

  • results = list(set(results))

A set has no order. The sort is complete and correct, and then thrown away one line later, before anything is returned. Every result the user sees is in arbitrary hash order.

Measured, same index, same queries — local ranking with that line removed versus the deployed API:

  • longest palindromic substring → the exact problem ranks 1st locally, 248th of 704 live
  • two sum → 112th locally, 6,008th of 9,008 live
  • output → 25th locally, 11,485th of 11,970 live

So the retrieval works and the product doesn't. The intent behind the line was real — the same link and title pair can be built twice — but dedup belongs in a pass that preserves order, and on this corpus it collapsed about 50 duplicates out of 9,008 while randomising all 9,008. It is the cheapest fix in the repo and the one with by far the largest effect.

The normalisation, and two lines that misfire

Cleaning a document lowercases it, cuts everything after the examples, strips digits and punctuation, collapses whitespace, drops stop words and filler words, and drops words shorter than three characters.

The example-stripping never fires. The text is lowercased on the line before the split, and the split looks for "Example 1" with a capital E. Nothing matches, so nothing is cut — 8,617 of 12,297 documents still contain the word "example", and every sample input and output is in the index. It is one character of casing, and the effect is that a large fraction of the indexed text is boilerplate that no useful query targets.

Digit-stripping was applied to the titles too. Removing digits makes sense for the index body, where a literal 10^9 is noise. It was also run over the displayed problem names, so 6,328 of 12,297 titles are visibly damaged: "Number of 1 Bits" renders as Number of Bits, "Search a 2D Matrix II" as Search a D Matrix II. Not one title in the file contains a digit. This is the second user-facing defect, and unlike the ranking one it is visible in a screenshot.

Two consequences of the same cleaning worth naming as design gaps rather than bugs:

  • No stemming. array has 2,912 postings and arrays has 545, as unrelated terms. Searching one silently misses most of the other.
  • The query is cleaned differently from the corpus. Documents lose punctuation and digits; the query is only lowercased and split. So two-sum and 3sum and 2 are not in the vocabulary and can never match anything. The two paths must share one normaliser — that they don't is the kind of bug that only shows up as "sometimes it finds nothing".

The result wire format

Each result is link + "*" + title in one string, split on * in the browser. It works because URLs and problem titles don't contain asterisks — a property of the current corpus, not a guarantee, and a title containing one would silently truncate. Two JSON fields cost nothing and remove the assumption. The titles also arrive with a trailing newline that the front end never trims.

A latent alignment risk

The indexer builds the document list, the link list and the title list in separate loops over the same numeric range. The document loop catches read failures and skips — appending nothing. The link and title loops have no such guard.

So a missing content file would leave the document list one shorter than the other two, and every document index past that point would resolve to the wrong problem's URL — a silent, total corruption of the results with no error anywhere. It hasn't happened, and the reason is upstream: the crawler numbers files contiguously because it only advances its counter on success, so the ranges are dense. All three lists are 12,297 long today. The safety is real but accidental, and it is one shared loop away from being structural.

What I would change

  • Delete the set() dedup and dedup with an order-preserving pass. One line, and the product starts working.
  • Fix the title mangling — never digit-strip display text; keep the raw title beside the cleaned one.
  • Hold the index in a long-lived process instead of spawning Python per request, and stop loading the 15 MB corpus file the query path doesn't read. That is the six seconds.
  • Share one normaliser between indexing and querying, and add stemming.
  • Return top-k and filter by platform server-side rather than shipping 12,000 rows to the client.
  • Replace the bare except that exits 0 — a failure should be a non-zero exit and a logged reason, not an empty success.
  • Reuse one browser across the crawl rather than launching 12,297 of them, and time the crawl so there is a number to improve.
  • Weight the title. Nothing distinguishes a term in the problem name from a term buried in the constraints, which is most of why two sum ranks the actual problem 112th even with a correct ordering.

SDE.name: Seat Reservation Bot
SDE.description: A 187-line Selenium script that clicked through an office seat-booking portal so a repeated two-desk reservation took no clicks — and a lesson in how quietly UI automation expires.
SDE.overview:
The office seat-booking portal took about ten clicks to say the same thing every day. Same floor, same two desks, next working day. This is the script that clicked them instead — and it is a script, not a system.

Worth being exact about what it does, because it is small. It launches Edge, dismisses the entry modal, walks the date picker forward until it finds a target month, selects a day, opens a floor card, clicks two seats by number, then presses Reserve and Confirm. That is the entire program: one file, one function, 187 lines. No configuration, no scheduling, no notifications, and no credential handling — it assumes a browser that is already signed in.

It no longer runs, and that is the part worth keeping. The target month is a string literal in the source, and the date loop only ever navigates forward — so run today, it walks the calendar away from the date it wants until a selector times out and a catch-all handler prints something unhelpful. It never had a way to recognise "the date I am looking for is behind me" as different from "the page is broken".

Underneath that, the deeper reason it was always going to expire: all 13 of its selectors are generated class names from the portal's component library — paper elevations, icon buttons, day-with-margin. Those are implementation details of somebody else's front end, not anything it promised to keep stable.

What I would flag reviewing it now:

  • A guard checks for at least three cards and then indexes the fourth, under a comment claiming it takes the third. All three disagree, and on a floor with exactly three cards it throws.
  • The loop over the two seats iterates a list whose values it never reads — both seat numbers are hardcoded in the body, so the booking sequence runs twice instead of once per seat. The loop variable is decorative.
  • Fixed sleeps are interleaved with proper explicit waits, which makes it both slower and less reliable than committing to either one.
  • Seat elements are located once and clicked twice, across a DOM the first click changes — a stale-reference bug waiting for the right timing.
  • The Dockerfile cannot work. It installs Selenium onto a slim Python image with no browser and no driver, to run a script that asks for Edge and then blocks on input() waiting for a keypress that will never come.

The honest verdict: it saved a couple of minutes a day for a few weeks, and taught me something that outlasted it. UI automation borrows an interface rather than being given one, so it has no contract and therefore no way to fail loudly — it expires quietly and waits for a human to notice. Given the same chore now I would find the request the page makes and call that directly, or accept the ten clicks.

This entry replaces an earlier description that credited the script with scheduling, notifications and availability search it never contained.

Source

SDE.name: App-Gen
SDE.description: A web-based utility that automates the creation of full-stack applications.
SDE.content:
Overview

AppGen is a powerful web-based utility that automates the creation of full-stack applications. By taking a JSON data model as input, it generates a frontend, backend, and database for a fully functional CRUD application. The generated source code is packaged into a ZIP file, complete with a Dockerfile and deployment instructions, allowing users to easily build and deploy their application as a Docker container.

Problem It Solves

Developing a CRUD-based application from scratch requires setting up a frontend, backend, and database, which can be time-consuming and repetitive. AppGen automates this process, significantly reducing development time and effort. With just a JSON data model, developers can instantly generate a working application, download the source code, and deploy it effortlessly.

How It Works

  • Input: The user provides a data model in JSON format that defines the structure of the application.
  • Code Generation: AppGen automatically generates:
    • Frontend: Built with React.js
    • Backend: Developed using Node.js
    • Database: Schema and queries for MariaDB
  • Packaging & Delivery:
    • The generated application is bundled into a ZIP file
    • The ZIP includes a Dockerfile and setup instructions
    • A download link is provided for the user to access their code

Technologies Used

  • Frontend: React.js
  • Backend: Node.js
  • Database: MariaDB
  • Deployment: Docker

Future Enhancements

AppGen is designed to be extensible, with the potential to support additional technologies, including:

  • Frontend: Angular, Vue.js
  • Backend: Java, Python, Go
  • Database: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB

With its ability to automate and accelerate web app development, AppGen is an ideal tool for developers looking to quickly scaffold applications while maintaining flexibility for further customization. 🚀

SDE.name: Time-Spent Chrome Extension
SDE.description: A Chrome extension to track time spent on different websites.
SDE.content:
Overview

The Time Spent Chrome Extension helps users track the amount of time they spend on various websites, providing insights into browsing habits.

Latest Version: 0.2.0 (Released on 17-09-2023)

New features added in this release:

  • 📊 Top 5 Most Visited Websites: View a list of the websites where you have spent the most time.
  • 📅 Date-wise Time Tracking: Track time spent on different websites for specific dates using the Select Date menu.

Problem It Solves

Many users are unaware of how much time they spend on different websites. This extension provides real-time insights into browsing behavior, helping users:

  • Improve productivity by identifying time-wasting websites.
  • Manage screen time more effectively.
  • Gain a better understanding of daily web usage trends.

How It Works

  1. The extension automatically tracks time spent on different websites.
  2. Users can view their browsing history in an intuitive dashboard.
  3. Data can be analyzed based on daily usage or cumulative top websites.

Project Links

  • GitHub Repository: View on GitHub

Project Contributor

👤 Name: Anuj Verma

🏫 Institute: IIT Kharagpur

👥 Team: Individual

This extension is perfect for professionals, students, and anyone looking to optimize their online time management. 🚀

SDE.name: Multilingual Stream Pipeline
SDE.description: A live sports feed dubbed into five languages as it plays — transcribed with Whisper, translated per language, re-voiced with TTS, mixed over stadium audio and muxed back into multi-audio HLS with frame-accurate subtitles. Built on the Event Exchange Framework.
highlights: Built a real-time dubbing pipeline that transcribes live match commentary, translates it into five languages, re-voices it with TTS and muxes the result back into multi-audio HLS with frame-accurate subtitles.
Designed the fan-out/barrier topology: five independent language lanes reconverge on a muxer that gates each segment on a Redis completion hash, so no segment ships with a missing audio track.
Preserved MPEG-TS presentation timestamps end to end and anchored WebVTT with X-TIMESTAMP-MAP so subtitles stay locked to the picture across every encode and mux stage.
Cut dub overrun by predicting synthesised speech duration with a regression model before the TTS call and compressing the translation against a syllables-per-second budget when it would overshoot.

Added an independent highlights branch on the same ingest topic — video-understanding model for detection, a second model to reject false positives, clips uploaded to S3 — isolated so it cannot affect the dubbing path.
SDE.overview:
A live football match is dubbed into five languages while it is still being played. Commentary arrives as part of a live video feed, and roughly a dozen seconds later the same match is going out with Hindi, Bengali, Gujarati, Marathi and Malayalam audio tracks and matching subtitles — none of which existed when the ball was kicked.

The chain per language is: hear it, write it down, translate it, say it in a synthetic voice, mix that voice over the real stadium noise, and glue it back onto the video without the lips and the words drifting apart. Doing that once, offline is a scripting exercise. Doing it continuously, for five languages at once, on a feed that never pauses, is the actual problem.

It is built on the Event Exchange Framework — my own event-streaming platform — using its "minion" model, where each stage is a container running the same generic runtime and differing only in a mounted rules file and config.

  • 5 target languages, each an independent lane — translation, speech synthesis, and its own subtitle track
  • 13 processor services across transcription, translation, speech, muxing and highlights
  • Whisper for transcription, LLM translation per language, ElevenLabs and OpenAI for voice
  • A separate AI branch that watches the same feed and cuts highlight reels on its own

Client and broadcaster names are omitted throughout — the real deployment carries a rights-holder and four named broadcasters.
SDE.hld:
The pipeline is a chain of Kafka topics with one structural feature that shapes everything else: it fans out to five language lanes and then has to put them back together again.

Why the barrier is the hard part

Each language lane runs at its own speed. An LLM translation takes as long as it takes; a speech synthesis call takes as long as it takes; Hindi and Malayalam have no reason to finish together. But the output is a single video segment carrying all the audio tracks, so segment 412 cannot be assembled until every language has produced its copy of segment 412.

That makes the muxer a barrier. It doesn't consume a queue and work; it waits. Each finished track writes a field into a Redis hash keyed by match and segment number, and the muxer proceeds only when the field count equals the configured track total — and only if that segment isn't already in a "done" set, so a duplicate delivery can't mux the same segment twice.

The consequence is the honest tradeoff of the design: the slowest language sets the latency for everybody. Adding a sixth language cannot make the output faster and can easily make it slower. That's the price of shipping one stream with every track in it rather than one stream per language.

Buffering: why four segments, not one

The receiver doesn't publish a segment the moment it lands. It holds a rolling window of four segments and publishes them together, and the transcriber transcribes the whole window but keeps only the words belonging to the middle segment.

This is a deliberate accuracy-for-latency trade. Speech recognition is much worse at a hard cut — a word split across a segment boundary is a word it gets wrong, and football commentary is full of names it can only resolve from surrounding context. Giving it roughly twenty-four seconds of continuous audio and then trusting only the centre means every word is transcribed with real context on both sides. The cost is paid once, in fixed delay, rather than continuously in mistranscribed names.

Failure behaviour

Every stage is separated from the next by a topic, so a stage that dies comes back and resumes from its committed offset rather than losing the backlog. A rules failure doesn't kill the consumer: the original message is republished to that service's retry topic and the loop continues, so one malformed segment cannot wedge a language lane.

Segment numbering survives restarts through Redis — the receiver reads the last media sequence back on startup and continues from it, instead of restarting at zero and producing a playlist that jumps backwards.

Delivery has its own health notion. The processes that re-encapsulate the output for each broadcaster parse their own encoder progress, and exit deliberately when throughput drops below three-quarters of the expected frame rate, letting the container restart policy rebuild the connection. A stalled-but-alive encoder is worse than a dead one, because nothing downstream notices.

Configuration as the unit of change

Almost every processor is the same container image. A translator and a speech synthesiser differ by the rules file and config mounted into them, not by their runtime. Config is loaded into Redis at startup and read from there, so a running service can be repointed without a rebuild, and the set of live services is inspectable because each one registers itself and cleans up its own keys on shutdown.

Adding a language is therefore a directory, two topics and a compose entry — no new program.

Three things hang off the side

Beyond the dubbing path, the same material feeds three services that the live pipeline never waits on.

Highlight reels come from a branch reading the same receiver topic as the transcriber, sharing nothing else with it. It accumulates a much longer window, sends the stitched video to a video-understanding model to find goals and near-misses, has a second model re-check the result to throw out false positives, and uploads what survives. Because it is a separate consumer group it can fall behind, fail, or be switched off entirely and the dubbing pipeline never notices — which is exactly why it hangs off a topic rather than being bolted into the transcriber.

A full-match highlights cut is assembled on request from the clips that branch produced, concatenated in order with a broadcast bumper spliced onto both ends.

Match reports are the neatest reuse in the project. The report service takes the subtitles the pipeline has already produced as its source, feeds the stitched commentary to a language model, and writes a written match report from it — then translates that report into ten languages. The live path's byproduct becomes another product's raw material at no extra cost to it.

Its one genuinely clever step is proper-noun correction. Speech recognition reliably mangles player names, and a match report full of misspelt footballers is worthless. So the model is handed a search-grounded squad list for the fixture and told to correct names against it before writing — repairing upstream transcription errors at the point where they would actually be noticed, rather than trying to make the recogniser perfect.
SDE.lld:
Keeping subtitles on the video

This is the part that looks trivial and isn't. Subtitles are published per segment, but a player needs to know where a segment's cue times sit on the video's timeline, not on a timeline starting at zero.

MPEG-TS timestamps run on a 90 kHz clock — 90 ticks per millisecond. Each subtitle file is written with cue times relative to its own segment, plus a header line anchoring local zero to that segment's real presentation timestamp:

  • X-TIMESTAMP-MAP=LOCAL:00:00:00.000,MPEGTS:<start_ms × 90>

For that anchor to be true, the original timestamps have to survive every single media operation in the pipeline. Which is why -copyts and -mpegts_copyts 1 appear on every encoder invocation — segmenting, audio extraction, speech alignment, muxing. Miss them once and that stage helpfully resets timestamps to zero, the anchor becomes a lie, and subtitles drift against the picture in a way that looks like a subtitle bug but is actually a muxing bug several stages upstream.

The full journey of one timestamp: source PTS → preserved through segmentation → read back out with a probe in milliseconds → carried on the Kafka message → added to the word offsets the recogniser returns → subtracted again to make cue times segment-relative → multiplied by 90 to write the anchor.

Making a translation fit the time it has

A sentence translated into another language is a different length, and a dub has a fixed slot: the segment it belongs to. Overrun and either the audio is cut off or it walks into the next segment.

The Hindi lane is the one built out furthest, and handles this in three stages:

  • Translate in a commentary register — native script, but keeping the English football loanwords commentators actually say rather than "correct" translations nobody uses.
  • Predict the spoken duration before synthesising it, using a small regression model trained on text features. If the prediction overruns the English source by more than a couple of seconds, the text is sent back to be compressed — rewritten shorter against a syllables-per-second budget. This is the interesting bit: it fixes length before spending an API call, rather than generating audio and discovering it doesn't fit.
  • Tag for delivery — emotion markers the voice model understands, chosen from match intensity measured as a rolling words-per-second window, with recent context read back so the same tag isn't repeated every segment.

The other four lanes are single-stage translation and take the simpler route: if the synthesised audio overruns, it is sped up with a filter, capped at 1.2× so it never becomes a chipmunk.

Stitching speech into a fixed slot

Synthesised phrases don't add up to exactly one segment. The gaps between them are adjustable and the segment length is not, so the audio is assembled in two passes: first absorbing any carry-over left by the previous segment, then shrinking the silences if the total still overruns. Anything that still doesn't fit becomes carry-over for the next segment — with a hard cap, because an uncapped carry-over is a slow drift that gets worse for the whole match.

The synthetic commentary is mixed against the real stadium audio rather than replacing it: crowd noise ducked, commentary lifted. Losing the stadium is what makes a dub feel like a voiceover instead of a broadcast.

Output and delivery

The final stage writes the media playlist, the per-language subtitle playlists and a master playlist advertising the audio and subtitle tracks. Segment durations are measured with a probe rather than assumed, because a playlist whose declared durations don't match its segments desynchronises players slowly.

Every playlist write is atomic — written to a temporary file, flushed, then renamed over the target. Players poll these files constantly, and a non-atomic write means eventually serving a half-written playlist to somebody.

From there the output is served over HTTP by a small nginx cluster and separately re-encapsulated to SRT per broadcaster. The cache policy splits the two kinds of file: playlists are explicitly uncacheable because they change every few seconds, while the video segments are immutable once written and cached hard. Getting that backwards is either a stale-playlist bug or a pointless origin hammering.

Adaptors

A set of small single-purpose services around the edges: protocol conversion into and out of the pipeline, and a time-shifted output that republishes the playlist a fixed number of segments behind live. The delay is done by rewriting sequence numbers, which is cheap and correct as long as segments are uniform — and they are, because the segmenter forces keyframes at segment boundaries.

What I would change

  • The barrier has no timeout — one permanently stuck language lane stalls output for every language. It should degrade to shipping the tracks that are ready and backfill, rather than blocking.
  • Two copies of the logic exist: the built image and the volume-mounted runtime copy that overrides it. Convenient for hot-fixing mid-match, but the two drift and the running copy is the only one that's true.
  • Several long-running services rely on the container restart policy rather than their own recovery loop — restart-as-error-handling works until the thing that failed is the restart.
  • Encoder settings are nominally variable bitrate but set to identical target and maximum, so they are constant bitrate with extra steps.
  • Credentials sit inline in service configs; they belong in injected secrets.

SDE.name: Sports Intelligence Console
SDE.description: The control plane for the multilingual streaming pipeline. Operators create a match from a form and the backend generates a whole per-match pipeline stack from templates — stream-scoped Kafka topics, processor configs, compose file — then runs and supervises it. Replaced a workflow that needed a developer on the server.
highlights: Built the control plane that replaced hand-operated streaming deployments: operators create a match from a form and the backend generates a complete per-match pipeline stack from templates, then runs and supervises it.

Designed stream-scoped naming for Kafka topics, consumer groups, processor directories and containers so multiple matches run concurrently on shared infrastructure without consuming each other’s segments.
Derived the entire inter-service wiring contract from a single language list, replacing ~50 hand-typed topic literals whose only guarantee of agreement was that the same string had been typed twice.
Split pipeline creation from execution across two endpoints so a misconfiguration produces an inspectable file rather than a half-started stack, and matches can be prepared well ahead of kickoff.
Added role-based access, token refresh with enforced password expiry, and live container stats and log streaming over sockets — removing SSH from the day-to-day operating loop.
SDE.overview:
The streaming pipeline used to be operated by hand. Running a match meant a developer on the server: editing config files, wiring Kafka topic names so services could find each other, bringing containers up in the right order, and tailing logs over SSH when something stalled. One match at a time, and only by someone who knew the whole system.

This console is what replaced that. An operator fills in a form — who's producing the feed, which fixture, what protocol comes in, which outputs go out — and the backend generates an entire pipeline stack from templates and runs it. No file editing, no SSH, and no requirement that the person running the match be the person who built the pipeline.

The key move is templatisation. The pipeline stopped being a hand-maintained deployment and became a shape that gets stamped out per match, so several matches can run side by side without their services colliding.

  • Create a match from a form; the backend writes a per-stream compose file and a full tree of processor configs
  • Run, stop, restart individual services from the browser, with live logs and container stats streamed back
  • Three roles — admin, developer, viewer — so operating a match no longer requires the keys to everything
  • Clients modelled properly — agency, tournament, match — instead of living in someone's config file

The console never touches a video frame. It is a code generator and a process supervisor; the actual transcoding, translation and dubbing happen in the pipeline it starts.
SDE.hld:
The console has one job that matters and it is not the UI: it turns a form submission into a set of files on disk that constitute a working pipeline, then hands them to Docker. Everything else — auth, roles, clients, log streaming — exists to make that job safe to hand to someone who isn't a developer.

Generation is separate from execution

Creating a stream and running one are two different requests. Create validates the input, renders templates, rewrites configs and writes a compose file — and stops. Nothing is started. A second, explicit call brings the stack up.

That split is worth the extra step. Generation is the part that can be wrong in interesting ways, and separating it means a bad config produces a bad file you can read rather than a half-started stack you have to tear down. It also makes creating a match well ahead of kickoff a normal thing to do — the stack sits on disk, generated and inspectable, until someone presses run.

Why every match needs its own names

The services in the pipeline find each other purely by Kafka topic and consumer-group name. There is no service discovery: a translator knows its input because a string in its config says so.

That makes the naming convention the entire wiring contract — and it means two concurrent matches using the same names would silently consume each other's segments. So every generated stack gets stream-scoped names: the topics, the consumer groups, the processor directories and the container names all carry the stream id. Isolation comes from the naming scheme rather than from separate infrastructure, which is what allows several matches to share one Kafka cluster.

There's a nice piece of engineering history in that file. The naming used to be roughly fifty hand-typed template literals across a config table — the same topic name written six times, a translator and its speech service sharing a consumer group only because the identical string had been typed twice. It's now derived from a single list of languages, so adding a language touches one array and the folder names cannot drift from the config table. That's the difference between a convention and a contract.

Supervising something that isn't yours

The console shells out to the host Docker CLI rather than driving a Docker library. The containers it starts are therefore siblings on the host daemon, not children of the backend — which has a consequence that is the single most common way this system breaks.

The backend writes compose files at a path inside its own container, but the bind-mount strings baked into those files have to be host paths, because the daemon resolving them lives on the host. Two different path roots for the same directory. If they drift apart the generated pipeline starts perfectly and mounts empty directories — the worst failure shape available, because nothing errors.

Access, and why roles were the point

The original workflow had exactly one privilege level: shell access to the server. The console splits that into admin, developer and viewer, so someone can watch a match run without being able to delete it.

Auth is a short-lived access token with a refresh token in an httpOnly cookie, and password expiry is enforced as middleware — an expired password blocks every route except changing it, rather than being a warning the UI could skip.

Live feedback

Container stats are pushed to the browser on an interval over a socket, and log streams are subscribed per stream. This is the part that replaced tailing files over SSH, and it is why the console can be the only place an operator needs to look.

Infrastructure health — broker, cache, proxy, the transcription hosts — is polled and shown as a strip across the top, because "is my match broken or is the cluster broken" was previously a question only a developer could answer.
SDE.lld:
What one "create" actually produces

A create request runs three generators over the same validated config:

  • Template copy — the runtime templates for receivers, processors and senders are copied into a stream-scoped directory, with generic folder names rewritten to carry the stream id, so hindi-translator becomes hindi-translator-<id>.
  • Config rewrite — every processor's config is rewritten in place with its stream-scoped consume topic, produce topic and consumer group.
  • Compose generation — a per-stream compose file is emitted, referencing the copied folders and the prebuilt processor images.

All three write into one directory named for the stream. Deleting a match is the mirror image: stop the stack, clean its Kafka topics and cache keys, take the compose down with its volumes, remove the network, then delete the directory.

The interlaced frame-rate doubling

My favourite piece of accumulated knowledge in this codebase, because it looks exactly like a bug.

The operator enters the source frame rate. When the input is flagged interlaced, the generated config gets double what they typed. That is deliberate. The receiver's default deinterlacing mode emits a frame per field, so a 25fps interlaced feed genuinely arrives downstream at 50fps — and the delivery service's health monitor kills its container when throughput falls below three-quarters of the configured rate. Passing the operator's 25 through unchanged would make every interlaced stream restart-loop forever.

Two numbers in two different services that must be changed together, with the reason living in a comment. It's the kind of coupling that only survives if it's written down.

Handling a secret you have to keep

Encrypted inputs take a passphrase, and it needs a specific set of behaviours:

  • Assembled into the connection string in one place, shared by both connection modes so they cannot drift, and emitting nothing at all when encryption is off — the unencrypted address had to stay byte-identical to what it was before the feature existed.
  • Stripped on the way out, not on the way in. The sanitiser sits at the read-response boundary rather than in the data layer, because the update path re-reads the stored record to merge changes — sanitising deeper would silently wipe the stored passphrase on every edit.
  • A blank passphrase on update means keep the existing one, not clear it.
  • Validation errors never echo the submitted value, and log lines on that path redact it.

Stack

Node and TypeScript on the backend, layered routes → controllers → services → repositories over a relational store, with the stream service as the orchestrator. React with Redux Toolkit on the front, plus a socket connection for stats and logs. The generated pipelines are Python services from the streaming project, which this console configures but does not contain.

What I would change

  • The stream service and its controller have grown into thousand-line god objects; new logic belongs in the focused generator classes beside them, and the existing bulk should follow.
  • There is no schema migration story — the ORM only syncs when the tables are missing, so adding a column does nothing to a live database until someone alters it by hand.
  • Endpoint paths are declared in three places, one of which is a partial duplicate. One should be canonical.
  • Two UI kits are installed and both are used depending on the file. Pick one.
  • Credentials are committed in plaintext across compose files and service configs; they belong in injected secrets, and the committed ones should be treated as burned.
  • There are no tests of any kind — the only automated checks are the type checker and the frontend linter.

SDE.name: DFB Analytics Dashboard Automation
SDE.description: A web automation project to scrape and analyze football match data from the DFB analytics dashboard, providing insights and visualizations.

SDE.name: Recon+ Framework
SDE.description: A metadata-driven data reconciliation framework: the datasets to compare, the key columns, and the checks to run are rows in a database, not code. Airflow builds the task graph from those rows and Spark runs the comparison.
highlights: Built a metadata-driven reconciliation framework where the pipeline is configuration rather than code: an Airflow DAG reads a 13-table metamodel and expands its own task graph, so onboarding a dataset is an insert rather than a deployment.

Designed the extension seams — an abstract check interface, an engine-agnostic dataframe wrapper, a connection factory and a pluggable execution-engine registry — so a new data-quality check is one class and a new storage backend is one adapter.

Shipped Spark jobs through Livy with the framework and its entire Python environment staged in object storage, keeping the cluster unmodified and making a framework release a zip upload rather than an image rebuild.
Separated a failing check from a failing job: mismatches and misconfigurations are reported as FAILED and SKIPPED results, so a partial run still publishes every table it did reconcile.

Wrote the reporting layer to two Elasticsearch indices — a summary per check and row-level detail only on failure — bounding write volume on clean runs while keeping failures fully diagnosable in Kibana.
SDE.overview:
Two systems hold what is supposed to be the same data, and somebody has to prove it. A feed lands from an upstream system; it gets loaded into a warehouse table. Recon+ is the thing that checks the two actually agree — and, when they don't, says which rows, which columns, and by how much.

The part that makes it a framework rather than a script is that the pipeline isn't written in code. Which datasets to compare, which columns form the key, which checks to run against which table, where the credentials live — all of it is rows in a database. Onboarding a new dataset is an insert, not a deployment. The Airflow DAG contains no table names at all; it reads them.

  • 6 built-in checks — duplicate keys, field-level value mismatches, row-count drift, missing mandatory fields, data-type mismatches, value-range validation
  • 13 metamodel tables holding clients, pipelines, blocks, tables, column mappings and check assignments
  • Airflow builds the task graph, Spark does the comparison, Elasticsearch and Kibana hold and show the results
  • Written to be extended — a new check is one class implementing one method; a new storage backend is one adapter

Client and dataset names are omitted throughout; the real deployment is configured per client entirely through metamodel rows.
SDE.hld:
The system splits cleanly in two, and the split is the design: Airflow decides what to run by querying a database, and Spark runs it. Neither half knows anything hardcoded about the data.

The DAG is a reader, not a definition

A run is triggered with two values — a client id and a pipeline id. Everything else is discovered. The DAG then does three successive queries, and expands a new set of tasks after each one using Airflow's dynamic task mapping:

  • Blocks — the ordered stages of this client's pipeline
  • Parent notebooks — which orchestrating modules those blocks need, found by joining blocks to tables to check assignments
  • Tables — which datasets each module owns, one mapped task each

Each stage is followed by a flatten-and-dedup step, because the joins legitimately return the same notebook or table more than once and mapping over duplicates would submit the same Spark job twice.

The consequence worth stating plainly: the task graph is a query result. The Airflow UI for a run with forty tables and a run with four looks structurally different, from the same unchanged DAG file. That is the feature, and it is also the debugging cost — you cannot read the DAG file and know what will run.

Why the framework travels through object storage

Spark jobs are submitted over the Livy REST API rather than spark-submit. That choice removes a whole class of coupling: the Airflow workers need only HTTP reach to Livy, not SSH keys for the cluster or a shared filesystem with it.

But it raises the obvious question of how the cluster gets the framework code. The answer is that it doesn't have it installed. Each submission points Livy at three artefacts in object storage: a small entrypoint script, the framework packaged as a zip on the Python path, and the entire Python environment as an archive, unpacked per job and pointed at with spark.pyspark.python.

So the cluster stays vanilla. Deploying a change to a check is re-uploading a zip — no cluster mutation, no image rebuild, and two clients can run different framework versions against the same cluster because the version is a path, not an installation.

The metamodel is read from inside Spark too

This is the part I would flag first in a design review. The Spark job does not receive a self-contained plan. It receives a table name and a config blob, and then calls back to the metamodel itself to fetch its column mappings, its key columns and its check list.

The upside is real: the DAG doesn't have to serialise a whole schema through Airflow's inter-task storage, and a mapping correction takes effect on the next run without redeploying anything. The cost is equally real — every concurrent Spark job is a concurrent client of one MariaDB instance. Table count scales the connection count, and that database is a synchronous dependency of work that is otherwise fully parallel. It is the first thing that would need to change to run this at ten times the width.

Concurrency: sequential where order matters, parallel where it doesn't

Blocks are ordered; tables are not. Blocks exist precisely to express "this group must finish before that one" — a warehouse layer can't be reconciled before the layer feeding it has been. So the block-resolution task is pinned to one instance at a time per run, while the table tasks fan out freely.

Inside a single Spark job there is a third level: the checks for one table run concurrently in a thread pool, sized from the client's own configured concurrency limit. Threads are appropriate here specifically because they aren't doing the work — each one submits Spark operations and waits.

Failure behaviour

The framework draws a hard line between a check that fails and a job that fails, and it matters more than it sounds.

A check finding a mismatch is a result: it returns a status of FAILED with its evidence, gets written to the report, and the pipeline carries on. A check that cannot run at all — no key columns configured, target dataset never loaded — returns SKIPPED rather than throwing, so a misconfiguration shows up as a visibly skipped check instead of a red Airflow task with a stack trace. Only infrastructure failure (metamodel unreachable, dataset missing, Livy session dead) raises.

Two more deliberate choices sit around that:

  • The terminal aggregation task runs on all_done, not on success. A run where three tables out of forty failed still completes and still reports the thirty-seven — a partial result is the normal case in reconciliation, not an exception.
  • Connections are closed in a finally block through the factory that owns them, so a job that dies mid-comparison doesn't leave the metamodel holding sockets. With every executor talking to one database, leaked connections would be the failure that takes down the next run rather than this one.

Results: two indices, and one of them is bounded

Every check emits a summary document — table, check, status, counts, timestamp, run id. Only failures additionally emit detail documents carrying the offending key values and the mismatched source and target values.

That asymmetry is the whole write-volume story. A clean run costs one small document per check regardless of dataset size; the expensive, unbounded output only exists where there is something to look at. Both indices carry the same derived join key, so a dashboard can move from "this check failed" to "here are the rows" without a foreign key.

Where it is designed to be extended

Four seams, in descending order of how well they hold up:

  • A new check — one class, one method, discovered by name from a metamodel row. This works; the six built-ins are all it knows about, and client logic drops in beside them.
  • A new storage backend — one adapter behind a common connection interface. Three exist (relational metamodel, object store, search index).
  • A new search-index version — version-specific adapters chosen at runtime from a config string, because the client library changed incompatibly across three major versions and the deployment target isn't always the same one.
  • A new compute engine — an abstract engine interface plus a factory registry. This is the seam that is declared more than it is built: four engines are named in the enum, one is implemented, and the other three raise. The abstraction is honest about its shape and dishonest about its coverage.
SDE.lld:
The check contract

A check implements exactly one method: it receives a dict holding config, a source dataset and a target dataset, and returns a dict. The return must carry the check's name, its id, and a status of PASSED, FAILED or SKIPPED. There is no second required method — an optional hook lets a check declare extra datasets it wants the parent to pre-fetch, and none of the built-ins use it yet.

Keeping the contract that small is what makes the framework's core promise true: a client writes a check without knowing anything about Airflow, Livy, the metamodel or the reporting layer.

Making checks engine-agnostic — and the escape hatch

Checks never receive a raw Spark DataFrame. They receive a wrapper exposing 15 members — count, filter, select, join, subtract, distinct, dedup, limit, collect, sample, cache, columns, dtypes, plus two purpose-built ones. The stated goal is that a check written today keeps working when the engine underneath changes.

The wrapper is not complete, and rather than pretend otherwise the codebase documents a single sanctioned way through it:

  • raw_df = df.df if hasattr(df, "df") else df

The duplicate-key check uses it, because grouping with Spark column expressions has no equivalent on the interface. I would rather have that one visible, greppable, documented line than an interface that quietly grows a Spark-shaped method every time someone needs one. But it is a debt, not a pattern: every use of it is a place the engine abstraction is a claim rather than a fact.

Two of the fifteen members exist for reasons worth spelling out:

  • Key sanitising replaces nulls and blank strings in key columns with a placeholder before any join. Without it, SQL null semantics silently drop exactly the rows most likely to be broken — a null key joins to nothing, so a reconciliation would report those rows as absent rather than as malformed.
  • Duplicate counting is on the interface rather than composed by callers, because group-count-filter is the single most repeated shape across the checks.

How one table is reconciled

Inside the Spark job, one module handles source-versus-target comparison and a second handles target-only validation. The source-versus-target one runs five phases:

  • Read configuration — the source/target mapping, the column-level mapping including which columns form the key, and the list of checks assigned to this table with their per-assignment parameters.
  • Load source — via a two-value feed type: a flat file in object storage, or a query against a relational source. An unrecognised value logs a warning and defaults to the relational path rather than failing.
  • Load target — from its own configured store.
  • Run the checks — concurrently.
  • Bulk-write the reports — once, for all checks together.

Both datasets are cached before dispatch. This is the detail that makes the thread pool worth having: six checks against one table share one materialisation of the data instead of re-reading it six times. Without the cache, concurrency would multiply the I/O it was meant to hide.

Check discovery, and why I'd change it

A metamodel row names a module. The parent imports it, walks its members, and takes the first class it finds that implements the check interface.

It works, and it means adding a check requires no registration step. It is also implicit in a way I don't like: put two check classes in one module and which one runs depends on member ordering, not on anything anyone wrote down. An explicit registry — a decorator, or a class name in the metamodel row — costs one line per check and removes the ambiguity entirely.

Connections and credentials

Connections come from a factory keyed on type + host + port + database and cached at class level, so the metamodel connection is opened once per job even though four separate phases ask for it. The whole cache is drained in a finally.

Credentials are never in the metamodel. The rows hold a secret ARN, resolved to a credentials dict at runtime, with three resolution paths in priority order: direct credentials passed in, an environment-backed sentinel for the metamodel itself, and ARN lookup for everything else.
