A single environment flag swaps ARN resolution for a local mock file, which is what makes the framework runnable on a laptop against Docker services with no cloud account.

Joining a result to its evidence

Summary and detail documents land in two different indices and need to be correlated in a dashboard. Each carries a join key: the SHA-256 of run_id : table_id : check_id : time, truncated to 8 bytes and base64url-encoded.

Hashing rather than concatenating keeps the key a fixed short width in every document and every dashboard filter. Truncating to 8 bytes is the questionable half — it is a deliberate size-over-safety trade with a real, if small, collision surface, and the un-truncated version it replaced is still sitting commented out above it. If two documents ever collide, a dashboard silently shows one check's rows under another's summary, which is precisely the kind of wrong that a reconciliation tool cannot afford. It should be wider.

What I would change

  • The metamodel queries are f-string interpolated, including values that arrive in the DAG run configuration. The caller is internal today, which is exactly the argument that stops being true later. These should be parameterised.
  • Nothing measures itself. The report has a duration field; no check populates it, so every document reports zero. The framework can tell you the data is wrong but not how long it took to find out — which is why this write-up carries no throughput figure.
  • The engine enum overpromises. Four engines declared, one implemented, three raising at run time. Either build them or shrink the enum to what exists.
  • One retry, no classification. A dead Livy session and a genuinely unreachable source get the same single retry. Those deserve different treatment: one is worth retrying immediately, the other never is.
  • Schema changes are hand-run SQL files. The metamodel is the whole product's configuration surface and it has no migration tooling — a new environment is a manual seed.
  • The join key should be wider than 8 bytes, per above.

3D.name: Taxi Rush
3D.description: A comprehensive taxi driver simulation game featuring real-time ride logic, economic management, and dynamic city navigation.
3D.content:
Taxi Rush is a mobile simulation game that gamifies the daily operations of a ride-hailing driver. It goes beyond simple driving mechanics to simulate the end-to-end service lifecycle, requiring players to manage time, fuel, and earnings within a realistic city economy.

Core Gameplay Loop

The game is built upon a robust GPS State Machine that mimics real-world apps like Uber or Rapido. Instead of just racing, the player engages in a strategic business management loop where every decision—from accepting a Ride Request to managing the Wallet Balance—impacts their ability to continue operating.

How It Works

  • Ride Allocation: A real-time request listener generates "Quest Cards" displaying pickup distance, estimated earnings, and time-to-accept.
  • Verification Logic: The OTP Handshake system forces a physical stop-and-interact moment, ensuring players confirm the passenger before the meter starts.
  • Dynamic Economy: A Surge Pricing System creates Heat Zones on the map, rewarding players for navigating to high-demand areas during rush hours.
  • Financial Constraints: The Wallet Lock mechanism monitors the driver's cash-to-digital ratio, disabling new rides if the commission debt exceeds the threshold.

Key Features & Systems

  • State Management: Distinct logic for Online, Pickup, En-Route, and Payment states
  • User Interface: Realistic notification cards with timers and route previews
  • Incentive Engine: Daily targets and quests to drive player retention
  • Frustration Mechanics: Realistic cancellation scenarios to add emotional stakes
  • Rating System: Post-ride feedback loop affecting driver reputation

This project demonstrates complex state logic implementation, UI/UX design for simulation, and game economy balancing, creating a polished experience that mirrors the real-world gig economy. 🚖
